graph_authoring_scope.aspect_description: Diagnosable concepts from The Economy Units 1-4: capitalism and long-run growth, technology and population, scarcity and individual choice, and strategic social interactions.
representative_tasks: Use a long-run GDP-per-capita graph to explain the hockey-stick pattern and identify what the graph does not prove.
Distinguish total GDP, GDP per capita, nominal income, and real income when comparing living standards.
Explain how private property, markets, and firms jointly characterize a capitalist economic system.
Compare markets and firms as alternative ways of coordinating specialization and production.
Explain how specialization and technological progress can raise labour productivity and living standards.
Interpret income-distribution data that show inequality both between countries and within countries.
Assess whether a correlation between capitalism and growth is sufficient evidence of causation.
Explain why environmental damage and inequality can coexist with rising average GDP per capita.
Reconstruct the feedback mechanism that produces a Malthusian trap.
Explain how sustained technological progress can allow income growth to outpace population growth.
Use relative wages and energy prices to predict whether a cost-saving technology will be adopted.
Distinguish a production function from a single observed production outcome.
Calculate and interpret average product and marginal product from a production schedule.
Identify diminishing marginal product and explain its relevance to production choices.
Use an isocost line to compare the costs of alternative production techniques.
Explain why an innovator may earn temporary economic rents after adopting a superior technology.
Explain how competition and diffusion can erode an innovator's temporary rents.
Distinguish a general-purpose technology from a narrow process improvement.
Evaluate competing explanations for why the Industrial Revolution began in Britain.
Identify which assumptions in a simplified technological-change model are doing explanatory work.
Construct a feasible set for a choice involving limited time and multiple objectives.
Identify the opportunity cost of additional consumption, study, leisure, or work in a concrete scenario.
Use an indifference curve to compare bundles without treating utility as directly measurable happiness.
Interpret the marginal rate of substitution as willingness to trade one objective for another.
Use a concave production function to explain why additional study or work may have diminishing returns.
Distinguish feasible, infeasible, dominated, and efficient choices on a constrained-choice diagram.
Find a preferred feasible choice by combining a feasible frontier with indifference curves.
Explain why a tangency condition characterizes an interior optimum and when it may fail.
Separate the income effect and substitution effect of an increase in the wage rate.
Explain why higher wages need not cause every person to work more hours.
Use ceteris paribus reasoning to evaluate a claim about study time and academic performance.
Identify omitted variables that could confound an observed relationship between effort and outcomes.
Compare average and marginal quantities and explain why they can move in different directions.
Explain scarcity as a constraint on choice rather than as a synonym for poverty.
Identify self-interest, altruism, reciprocity, and inequality aversion in a strategic interaction.
Represent a two-player interaction with actions, payoffs, and outcomes.
Determine whether a strategy is dominant by comparing payoffs across the other player's possible actions.
Find a Nash equilibrium and explain why it need not maximize joint wellbeing.
Explain the conflict between individual incentives and collective outcomes in a prisoner's dilemma.
Diagnose free riding in a public-goods game and identify the payoff structure that sustains it.
Predict how repeated interaction can change incentives for cooperation.
Explain how reciprocity and credible punishment may support cooperative outcomes.
Distinguish altruistic preferences from strategic cooperation motivated by future rewards.
Use inequality aversion to explain behavior that a purely self-interested model cannot explain.
Predict how changing a game's rules or payoffs can change its equilibrium.
Distinguish a coordination problem from a social dilemma using payoff comparisons.
Interpret experimental-game evidence without assuming that one observed choice reveals a fixed personality type.
Explain how institutions can alter incentives while preferences remain unchanged.
Design a diagnostic comparison that separates misunderstanding of Nash equilibrium from disagreement about fairness.
Connect capitalism, technological change, constrained choice, and social interaction without collapsing them into one causal claim.
excluded_topics: Units 5 and later of The Economy
Detailed firm governance and employment contracts
Credit, banking, money, inflation, unemployment, and fiscal policy
Advanced welfare economics and formal social-choice theory
Econometric estimation beyond qualitative ceteris paribus reasoning
Policy prescriptions not developed in Units 1-4
Historical facts that do not support a reusable economic concept
